observation.visible_scene: A single leafless tree rendered as a dark silhouette stands centered on a low, flat horizon line under a star-speckled night sky that grades from deep blue at the top to pale glow at the horizon. The lower half of the frame is a calm water surface that mirrors the tree and the sky; the mirrored tree appears as a wavy, broken reflection. The overall composition is symmetric about the horizon and stays fixed within the frame throughout the excerpt.
visible_changes: The tree, the horizon line, and the sky gradient remain in the same screen position across all frames, indicating no camera pan, tilt, or zoom.

The reflected tree shows only subtle, continuous deformation of its ripple pattern (the mirrored branches shift slightly in shape), consistent with gentle motion on the water surface rather than the reflection translating or the object moving.

Small bright glints/highlights appear and disappear at varying spots on the water (e.g., near the top of the reflection and to its left/right in different frames), indicating localized sparkle changes on the surface.
No object enters or leaves the frame; the silhouette tree does not change size, shape, or location, so there is no object movement distinct from the static scene.
The faint dots in the sky (stars) stay essentially fixed in position.
The water reflection never fully resolves into a sharp mirror image; its waviness persists as a persistent property.
outside_clip_unknowns: Whether the slight ripple motion is driven by wind or a current is not shown.
The light source producing the horizon glow and the surface glints is not visible.
Whether the small specks are stars, snow, dust, or compression noise cannot be confirmed from the frames alone.
Any motion before the first frame or after the last frame is outside the excerpt.
uncertain_details: The magnitude of the reflection's ripple deformation is small; it is hard to distinguish genuine water motion from encoding/compression flicker.
The apparent movement of the bright glints is sparse and may be partly artifact rather than a physical object moving.
Camera stillness is inferred from the constant framing of the tree and horizon; minor sub-pixel drift cannot be fully ruled out.
